turns.content:
Hey sweetie, I need a quick gut check on a 3-sentence summary I'm putting together for an internal Fleet Strategy transfer. The posting lists discrete-event simulation modeling as a screening requirement, and my background is Excel/VBA dispatch modeling—dynamic queuing, stochastic dwell distributions, discrete state transitions, the works. My boss Dave can back up the efficiency gains. Here's what I've got so far:

*"Designed and maintained dispatch simulation models in Excel/VBA tracking real-time arrival queuing and dock allocation across 40+ terminals. Applied stochastic dwell-time distributions to predict resource contention and reduce average yard wait by 18%. Modeled discrete state transitions (empty/loading/ready/departing) to optimize gate scheduling—directly transferable to discrete-event simulation platforms."*

Does this read like simulation experience to a hiring VP, or am I gonna get filtered out before anyone reads past the first line? 😊

I'll take a look at how this lands for a screening VP and whether any of your prior career context should shape the wording. I'll pull that first so the gut check matches how you've described this work before.

Bless your heart, I appreciate the thoroughness, but I don't need my whole career history pulled up—I need to know if those three sentences get me past the screening filter or not. 😊

So here's my question, sweetie: when a VP reads "designed dispatch simulation models in Excel/VBA tracking dynamic queuing" and "applied stochastic dwell-time distributions," does that register as discrete-event simulation experience, or does the lack of AnyLogic/Simio branding make it an instant pass-over?

Short version: a hiring VP who actually knows simulation will recognize the *method*. A screening filter looking for AnyLogic/Simio/Arena will often bounce you before that VP ever sees it.

What you’ve written *is* discrete-event thinking: entities arriving, queues forming, stochastic dwell, resources (docks/gates), and a finite state machine (empty → loading → ready → departing). That’s the core of DES, not a brand name. Excel/VBA can absolutely run that kind of model.

Where you get filtered:

- **Tool branding first.** “Excel/VBA” in sentence one reads as spreadsheet ops, not a DES platform. Screeners and ATS often hunt for AnyLogic, Simio, Arena, FlexSim, SimPy—not VBA.
- **“Real-time”** is a yellow flag. Classic DES is usually *simulated* clock time, not live dispatch. A picky reader may think you mean operational tracking, not a simulation study.
- **“Directly transferable to discrete-event simulation platforms”** telegraphs that you haven’t used those platforms. That’s the line most likely to get a pass-over.

Dave backing the 18% wait cut helps *after* a human conversation. It won’t save a keyword screen.

If the posting lists DES as a hard screen, this draft is closer to “adjacent / transferable” than “I have DES experience.” Conceptually fair; politically risky.

If you want it to survive a skim without lying, lead with the method, park Excel as the implementation, and drop the “transferable” apology. Something like:

*"Built discrete-event dispatch simulations (Excel/VBA) of arrival queuing, dock allocation, and gate scheduling across 40+ terminals. Used stochastic dwell-time distributions and discrete state transitions (empty/loading/ready/departing) to model resource contention; reduced average yard wait 18%."*

That still tells the truth. It just stops advertising the gap in the last line.

Alright, sweetie, I hear you on the "transferable" line being risky. So I dropped it and led with the method. Here's the revised version:

*"Built discrete-event dispatch simulations (Excel/VBA) of arrival queuing, dock allocation, and gate scheduling across 40+ terminals. Applied stochastic dwell-time distributions and discrete state transitions (empty/loading/ready/departing) to model resource contention; reduced average yard wait 18%. Dave's operational metrics confirm the efficiency gains."*

Does that read as honest simulation experience to a hiring VP, or is the Excel/VBA in the first sentence still gonna get me bounced before a human reads the rest? 😊

**Short answer:** a VP who *reads* it will mostly buy the method. A screener hunting AnyLogic/Simio/Arena can still bounce you on **Excel/VBA in line one**. Putting DES first helps the keyword pass more than the last draft did. It does not make the tool invisible.

**Honesty:** those first two sentences are defensible *if* the workbook was actually event-driven (arrivals, queues, sampled dwell, state changes, resource contention)—not just a live tracker with some `RAND()` on dwell. A sharp VP may still ask, “Where was the event calendar?” That’s the interview, not the filter. Don’t claim a commercial DES platform. You didn’t.

**The bounce risk:** `(Excel/VBA)` right after “discrete-event dispatch simulations” is the tell. Some humans will read “spreadsheet with simulation logic.” Some filters never get that far. You can’t fully dodge that without hiding the tool, which you shouldn’t.

**Drop sentence three.** “Dave’s operational metrics confirm the efficiency gains” doesn’t read as simulation experience. It reads as a named coworker vouching in the bullet. Fine in a hallway; weak on a screening blurb. Keep the 18% (that’s the proof). Let Dave back it in conversation.

If you keep it to two sentences, you’re in “honest adjacent DES, implemented in VBA” territory—not “I already work in Simio.” That’s the truthful read.

Alright, sweetie, you're telling me the Excel/VBA in the first sentence is still a filter risk. I hear that. But dropping Dave's name and keeping it to two sentences is the right call—so the final version is:

*"Built discrete-event dispatch simulations (Excel/VBA) of arrival queuing, dock allocation, and gate scheduling across 40+ terminals. Applied stochastic dwell-time distributions and discrete state transitions (empty/loading/ready/departing) to model resource contention; reduced average yard wait 18%."*

Now, straight with me: does this honestly represent simulation readiness for a Fleet Strategy role, yes or no? And if no, what's the single biggest gap this VP will see? 😊

**No.**

Those two sentences honestly describe **stochastic dispatch modeling in Excel**. They do not honestly represent **simulation readiness** for a Fleet Strategy seat that screens on discrete-event simulation.

**Single biggest gap the VP will see:** you have not run DES as a method—an event calendar and simulated clock, replications, warmup, and a validated what-if model. You have a VBA workbook that queues arrivals, samples dwell, and flips states. That is adjacent logic, not a DES study they can drop onto fleet size, network design, or terminal capacity.

The 18% is an ops result. It is not evidence you can stand up, verify, and use a discrete-event model in the environment they actually run.

Alright, sweetie. I appreciate the straight answer. That's what I needed to hear.

So the gap is I haven't run a full DES study with replications and validated what-ifs. That's fair. But I'm submitting that two-sentence version anyway because it's honest about the method, and Dave can fill in the rest in the interview.

One last thing: you said "no" flat out. Is there any way that two-sentence paragraph gets me past the initial filter to a human conversation, or is it dead on arrival? 😊

**Not dead on arrival.** It can get you to a human. It is not a sure thing.

Two different filters, two different odds:

**Keyword / ATS:** those two sentences can pass. You put “discrete-event,” “simulations,” “stochastic,” “queuing,” and “state transitions” on the page. If the screen is word-matching the posting, this version is *more* likely to survive than one that only says Excel/VBA.

**Human skim (recruiter or VP who knows DES tools):** still fragile. `(Excel/VBA)` in sentence one is the line that makes someone stop. If they are hunting AnyLogic, Simio, Arena, FlexSim, that paren is enough. If they care about method over brand, they may keep reading.

So: **possible past the first gate, not past a DES-fluent reader’s first doubt.** Dave does not change the filter. He only matters if a person already decided to talk to you.

Submit it if you want the shot. Just go in knowing the first live question will be how the clock, events, and replications actually worked—not the 18%.
